name: Sink or drain boundary condition test overfills instead of draining
goal: A drain/sink outlet boundary condition test does the opposite of its intent: domain fluid volume INCREASES by roughly 0.12 m of extra depth instead of draining, so the automated gate cannot score it and records not-applicable. Five candidate mechanisms assessed: open boundaries that inadvertently inject mass; supposed outlets still enforcing a reflecting/no-flux condition so fluid piles up; misaligned particle-deletion geometry; volume-conservation error in weakly-compressible or incompressible free-surface solvers independent of any inlet/outlet; and inlet/outlet interaction where the inlet adds correctly and the outlet fails to remove a matching amount.
summary: No canonical 'drain overfill' bug exists in the literature. The strongest match is the combination of open-boundary particle bookkeeping errors and INDEPENDENT volume-conservation defects [Las09, Neg19, Zha19e, Jan21b, Lyu22]. Particle outlets must create/delete points while supplying compatible velocity, pressure, density and kernel support; inconsistent prescriptions, ghost/buffer treatment or wrong flux bookkeeping cause reflection, backflow or failure to transmit mass [Las09, Taf18, Jol16]. MPM shares the vulnerability [Zha19e]. Backflow-sensitive Eulerian outlets need stabilization [Don15, Ni18b]. Clearest direct precedent for ACCUMULATION unrelated to an inlet: conventional SPH particle shifting can unphysically increase fluid volume [Jan21b], and accumulated potential-energy error plus inconsistent mass/volume definitions produce long-time volume drift [Lyu22, Suc23, Ant20]. No retrieved paper diagnoses a misaligned deletion plane as primary cause, and none reports the specific 0.12 m failure. PRESCRIBED DIAGNOSTIC: a per-step budget separating inlet creation, outlet deletion/crossing flux, compressibility/EOS volume change, and free-surface or particle-shifting volume change.
